summary: This RFC specifies using the SIP Call-Info header field to carry Rich Call Data about the originating party. It gives the receiving party a description of the caller, including information about the reason for the session.

eli5.summary: It is the place in a phone call's envelope where the caller's name and reason for calling get written, so your phone can show them.

questions: how does sip show caller details
what does the sip verified parameter mean
how long can a sip call-reason be
subtitle: How a SIP call can carry the caller's name, logo, photo and reason for calling in the Call-Info header.

tldr.problem: A phone number alone tells the person being called very little. The SIP display-name is often ignored, and the receiving side usually has to look the name up itself.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9796 defines how the SIP Call-Info header field carries Rich Call Data: a jCard describing the caller, an icon, a short call reason, and flags saying the data was verified and has an integrity hash.
tldr.outcome: A called device can show who is calling and why, and can tell whether the data was checked against a signed STIR RCD PASSporT. Without that signing, the receiver has to trust the network that delivered it.

today: RFC 9796 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used together with the STIR RCD PASSporT of RFC 9795.

sections.title: Why Call Info Needs Rich Data
sections.content:
Phone networks have long been able to deliver a calling name, but the receiving side often has to work it out from the calling number using an address book or an outside database. SIP can carry a display-name in the From header field, but the RFC notes that this field is not commonly trusted and is often replaced or ignored. The same is true of the Call-Info header field.

RFC 9796 defines a usage of Call-Info that carries Rich Call Data (RCD) about the originating party: information beyond the telephone number, such as a calling name, logo, photo, or jCard object, plus the reason for the call. It works alongside the STIR "rcd" PASSporT defined in RFC 9795.
sections.eli5: Caller ID usually shows just a number. This lets the call also say who is ringing and why, like a name tag on a visitor.

sections.title: The Call-Info Framework for RCD
sections.content:
The document adds one new purpose token, jcard, and three new Call-Info parameters: call-reason, verified and integrity. It also gives guidance on the existing icon token from RFC 3261, which points to an image that can be shown to the person receiving the request.

RCD is meant to be singular: the receiver should not have to choose between duplicate or conflicting RCD. It is added either by a party that is authoritative over the information, or translated from a verified STIR RCD PASSporT. Other parties in the call path MUST NOT modify the Call-Info header field or add further Call-Info header fields related to RCD.

The calling name itself is not carried here. As in RFC 9795, it comes from the display-name of the From header field, or sometimes from P-Asserted-ID (RFC 3325).
sections.eli5: Only the person who really knows the caller's details should write them on the envelope, and nobody else along the way may scribble on it.

sections.title: The jcard Purpose Token and Its Delivery
sections.content:
With purpose=jcard, the Call-Info URI points to a jCard JSON object (RFC 7095) with media type application/json in UTF-8. The jCard can be carried in three ways:

  • directly in the URI using the data URI scheme;
  • in the body of the SIP request, referenced with the cid URI scheme (RFC 2392);
  • at a URI whose transport can validate the integrity of its source, for example HTTPS tied to a specific validated domain.

A call and its RCD Call-Info header field MUST contain only a single jCard object, an array of two elements: the string "vcard" and then an array of properties. The calling name, logo or photo must be consistent with the SIP message, because the values in the RCD MUST match the corresponding SIP information so that verification works.
sections.eli5: The caller's business card can be taped to the envelope, tucked inside it, or left at an address you can visit. It must be just one card, and it must match what the envelope says.

sections.title: The New Parameters
sections.content:
call-reason is a short text for display while the phone rings. It SHOULD be no longer than 64 characters, and displays may truncate longer text. It is optional, and the sender cannot guarantee a display will support it. Strings that look like URIs or other 'clickable' actions are discouraged. The RFC chose a new parameter rather than the Subject header field because Subject has seen little use and its specification describes use in filtering.

verified has one valid value, true. It says the party that added the header field successfully performed the verification procedures from RFC 9795, and it applies only to the Call-Info header field it appears on. Recipients trust it only as far as they trust the party they received the request from.

integrity carries an integrity hash for the resource a URI points to, built as in the "rcdi" claim of RFC 9795. Implementations MUST support sha256, sha384 and sha512. When the "rcdi" claim was successfully verified, the header field should carry both verified and integrity.

Parameters that need no URI use the null data URI data:. The display-name in From or P-Asserted-ID is considered verified when the header has purpose=jcard, the URI data: and verified="true".
sections.eli5: There are three extra stickers. One says why the person is calling, one says a checker confirmed the details, and one is a fingerprint so you can tell if the picture was swapped.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The simplest header is Call-Info: <https://example.com/qbranch.json>;purpose=jcard, pointing to a jCard file. The RFC also shows full SIP INVITE requests using the data scheme and the cid scheme with a multipart/mixed body, each with a call-reason of "Rendezvous for Little Nellie".

Section 9 explains the typical flow. A terminating provider receives a request with a STIR RCD PASSporT in an Identity header, verifies it, and then extracts and translates the verified data into Call-Info header fields for the end device across the trusted User-Network Interface. That is why the header fields can carry verified and integrity values copied from the PASSporT.
sections.eli5: The phone company checks the caller's signed ID at the border, then copies the checked details onto a fresh envelope for your phone.

sections.title: jCard Properties and Media Rules
sections.content:
Section 10 picks a subset of vCard properties suited to telephone and messaging: identification (fn, n, nickname, photo), adr, communications (tel, email, lang), geography (tz, geo), organization (title, role, logo, org) and explanatory (categories, note, sound, uid, url, version). The version property MUST be included, with the value 4.0 in the examples.

  • Content referenced by URIs in a jCard MUST NOT itself contain URIs, and clients must not follow them.
  • Images SHOULD default to PNG or JPEG, and SVG Tiny 1.2 SHOULD be supported as an additional default. A photo SHOULD be square, at 128x128, 256x256, 512x512 or 1024x1024 pixels.
  • Image file names can end in -HxW before the extension to signal resolution.
  • A client MUST only display a url property, not follow it or preview it automatically.
  • Telephone numbers in tel are not part of STIR verification and need not match the PASSporT "orig" claim.
sections.eli5: There is a short list of things a card may say, and rules to keep it safe: show a web address but never open it for you, and send pictures in common sizes.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Revealing a person's name, location and affiliation carries privacy risk. Call-Info has no confidentiality of its own; transport-level security can hide it from eavesdroppers. Used alone, the specification assumes the called party's device can trust the SIP network to assign, deliver and protect the correct RCD. Because that trust cannot be guaranteed, the recommended approach is for the inserting entity to also sign the caller information using STIR and the "rcd" PASSporT of RFC 9795.

The RFC also warns that RCD can help impersonation if the ecosystem has no management and policy layer validating participants. Embedded media or remote URIs are a potential threat vector for crafted documents, and fetching a remote URI can expose information about the user or device. Some sensitive users may want to disable these mechanisms. Information in RCD should be considered public.
sections.eli5: A name tag is only as trustworthy as whoever wrote it, so a signed stamp is best. Pictures and links can also be tricky, so phones should be careful with them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has added this document to the references for the jcard value of the purpose parameter in the "Header Field Parameters and Parameter Values" registry. It also registers three Call-Info parameters in that registry (defined by RFC 3968): call-reason (a quoted string), verified (a quoted string that can only be "true") and integrity (a quoted string). Only verified has predefined values.
sections.eli5: The new words were written into the official dictionary of SIP so everyone spells them the same way.

items.desc: Only valid value is true; the sender verified the information.
